title: Names and vital statistics; early life and move to Idaho
description: Emma Christine Cook gives her name, birth date in 1906, and birthplace of Ward, Washington. She traces her family's moves through Farmington, La Crosse, and Lancaster, her marriage at seventeen, and the couple's 1930 journey through Deer Park and Brook to Neva Hill and finally Elk River, where John found work with Potlatch.

title: Depression years; building the house; jobs in later life
description: She recalls Depression-era scarcity while John moved between Potlatch, Diamond Match, and city maintenance, and describes how the two of them built a bedroom and dining room addition themselves. After John's stroke she took a kitchen job at the fire patrol camp, where she cooked and made sandwiches for firefighters and fire-school boys.

title: Getting to work without a car; kitchen memories
description: Cook explains that without a car after her husband's stroke she faced six daily trips, sometimes walking, and eventually quit the camp job she loved. She remembers the camp's generous provisions, its butcher and well-stocked cellar, and the hundreds of cold, hungry fire-school boys lining up to eat.

title: First arrival in Idaho; parents and family background
description: She retells how the family first came to Idaho in 1930 in an old Maxwell, getting lost near Deary on the way to Elk River. She then gives details on her mother Christine Dormier and father Henry Fromm, a German-Russian immigrant and rural mail carrier, and her mother's daily mail runs between depot and post office.

title: Childhood work and missing out on fun
description: Cook describes taking care of her seven younger siblings from age ten or eleven and helping her father cut and stack hay for the mail-route horses. She recalls missing Fourth of July outings and dances, resenting it then but understanding now that the family needed her labor.

title: Parents' and siblings' details; husband's background
description: She records her parents' birth, marriage, and death dates, names her two brothers and five sisters with their married names and homes, and describes her husband John Cook's birth in Austria, his immigration, and his many logging and road jobs, including hearing damage from dynamite.

title: Marriage and fiftieth anniversary; daughters
description: She recalls her Christmas Eve 1923 wedding in Colfax and the couple's fiftieth anniversary vow renewal in 1972, attended by family from as far as Sacramento. She names her three daughters, Jeannie, Norma June, and Marilyn, their birthplaces and dates, and Marilyn's civil-service post office job in Troy, Idaho.

title: Schooling and work history; quilting and crafts
description: Cook says she went only through eighth grade and clerked briefly in a store before marriage. She describes her hobbies of crocheting, sewing, piecing quilts, and making bead flowers and holiday figures, her reluctance to sell her work, and the difficulty of getting craft supplies in Elk River.

title: Country life tradeoffs; isolation and snow
description: She weighs the disadvantages of Elk River's snow, isolation, and dependence on borrowed cars against its cool, quiet summers. She tells of her husband's frightening nighttime illness, her wish to move nearer her daughter in the valley, and the zoning rules that have blocked placing a trailer house there.

title: Clubs, church, and raising children
description: She describes her long membership in the Rebekah lodge, which she resigned when it moved to Deary, her birthday club, and helping with a two-week summer Bible school. She contrasts her strict, work-centered childhood with the freedom she gave her own daughters, proud that all three graduated.

title: Logging camp life; women alone in Elk River
description: Isabel Miller recounts bringing a newborn home in the snow to a bare house in Elk River while her husband lived in Potlatch logging camps, coming home only briefly each weekend. She explains that this went on for decades until the camps closed in the late 1960s, leaving the town mostly women and children who had to fend for themselves, especially during forest fires.

title: Courtship; schooling; strict father
description: Miller tells how she courted her husband from age thirteen and married at seventeen, a restricted teenage life supervised by her mother. She describes her German father's belief that girls did not need education or their own money, her leaving school after eighth grade, and her dream of running away from a strict home.

title: Married life; children; sibling loyalty
description: Miller says marriage brought her freedom and happiness, and describes the births of her three daughters, spaced widely apart because her husband limited family size. She recalls with warmth how she and her seven siblings stuck together and protected each other against their strict father.

title: Childbirth; medical care in Elk River
description: Miller describes having her babies at home with doctors summoned from Troy and Bouleville, since the local hospital and doctor were gone, and her husband running miles from camp to arrive in time. She recalls staying with her sister in Indicot for one birth and the scarcity of medical help in Elk River.

title: Childrens recreation; town social life
description: Miller explains how her daughters amused themselves with homemade ice cream, dances, radios, paper dolls cut from catalogs, and books. Women with baby buggies formed a daily parade to the mail and the drugstore soda fountain, a social life she remembers fondly despite her husband's long absences.

title: Family celebrations; canning and gardening
description: Miller describes big family meals for birthdays, anniversaries, and Christmas, with sauerkraut and German dishes like sarmas. She cans heavily, including dozens of quarts of carrots, worries about the shortage of jar lids, and relies on neighbors for garden produce now that her husband Johnny can no longer work.

title: Injury and widowhood; financial insecurity
description: Miller talks about worrying through her husband's many logging injuries and what widows in Elk River did afterwards. Families survived without welfare by running up grocery credit, delaying rent, and borrowing money, so life then was far less secure than it is now.

title: Basketmaking; feeling needed
description: The interviewer demonstrates willow basketmaking, explaining the seasons for gathering material and selling baskets to Moscow shops and visitors. Miller reflects that she enjoys younger people coming to visit and wants to feel needed, dropping anything to help others.

title: Advice; later life; decisions
description: Miller says she would not wish her hard life on a young woman starting out but feels more secure now that her children are grown. She discusses her enjoyment of the news and quiz shows, and explains that her husband leaves almost all decisions, including finances, to her, a sharp contrast with her father's rule.

title: Mother's divorce; father's harshness
description: Isabel Miller expresses regret that her mother did not divorce her father while the children were still home. She describes her father's severity and suggests his temperament was linked to his German background.

title: World War II in Elk River; Mrs. Morris; women's war work
description: The conversation turns to the war years, which Isabel Miller remembers as a time of prosperity. She identifies longtime residents Mr. and Mrs. Morris and explains that she did not join women's wartime volunteer groups.

title: Staying in Elk River; selling the house; trailer option
description: Isabel Miller explains that her husband's work has kept them in Elk River but they now wish to move. She describes the challenges of selling their house and considers buying a trailer near her daughter in Detroit.

title: Husband's basket preoccupation; interview closes
description: Isabel Miller complains that her husband is absorbed in basket-making and offers little help with decisions. The interview concludes with signatures and release forms.
